q: Filing delay is used as a complete measure of tax compliance. What should be questioned?
options: Validity: timeliness captures only part of compliance.
The arithmetic definition of a mean.
Whether firm identifiers have a median.
why: A reliable timing measure can still miss registration, reporting or payment obligations.

q: Bars show 9.8 and 10.5 with a baseline of 9.7. What is the main problem?
options: Truncated bar lengths exaggerate the visual difference.
Every kind of graph always needs a zero baseline.
why: The values remain true, but full bar lengths should normally be measured from zero. The increase is 0.7, about 7.14%.

q: Multiple-response survey percentages total 140%. Which display is suitable?
options: Bars with the original respondent denominator.
why: Selections overlap. They are not mutually exclusive parts of one whole.

q: Unequal intervals have densities 1.8, 2.4 and 1.33. Which is the modal interval?
options: Whichever has the largest raw count.
why: For unequal widths, compare density. Histogram areas represent frequencies.

q: Grouped times have counts 8,15,12,5 in four consecutive 12-hour intervals. What is known?
options: The median lies in [12,24); interpolation needs an assumption.
The median must be in the most populated half of the last interval.
why: Cumulative counts 8,23,35,40 place the midpoint in the second interval. Uniform interpolation gives about 21.6.

q: Two ordinal distributions have the same modal category. Must they have the same median category?
options: Only if the category names are numbers.
why: The mode uses the largest frequency; the median uses order and cumulative frequencies.

q: Office rates are 8/10 and 45/90. What is the overall filing rate?

options: A position in the ordered observations.
why: Percentiles concern relative positions. Sample conventions and ties matter.

q: Why square deviations when calculating variance?
options: Signed deviations from the mean sum to zero.
Squaring preserves the original measurement unit.
why: Squaring avoids cancellation but produces squared units. SD restores the original unit.

q: For 20,40,0,70, the squared deviations total 2675. What is the sample variance?
why: The sample convention uses n−1. The average squared deviation with denominator n describes this observed set.

q: Multiplying every value by 1,000 changes variance by:
why: Variance scales by the square of the factor; SD scales by its absolute value.

q: With three equally frequent categories, Gini–Simpson and its normalised value are:
why: The raw maximum is 1−1/K; dividing by it gives the normalised maximum 1.

q: Changing Shannon’s logarithm base does what?
options: Changes raw entropy, while matched-base normalisation stays the same.
Changes neither the raw nor the normalised value.
why: The maximum is log K in the chosen base. Dividing numerator and denominator by the same base-conversion factor cancels it.

q: A large positive turnover z-score establishes:
options: A value above the reference mean, measured in SD units.
That the data are normally distributed.
why: A standardised distance neither proves wrongdoing nor establishes normality.
